title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Saying that something EXISTS splits by number: c'è for one thing, ci sono for more than one — C'è un libro sul tavolo · Ci sono due libri sul tavolo. English makes the same split with "there is" and "there are", so the agreement itself is a free ride; what is new is the two Italian words.
Where a thing IS takes essere, plainly: Il libro è sul tavolo. Italian has one verb for identity, origin and location alike, so there is no second "to be" to choose between.

A preposition fuses with a following definite article into ONE written word, and the fusion is compulsory: a + il = al, in + il = nel, su + il = sul, with the feminine partners alla, nella, sulla. There is no option to write them apart.

Prepositions stand in front of the noun, as in English: sul tavolo, sotto il tavolo, in cucina. Some places take no article at all — in cucina, a casa, in bagno — and those are learned as whole phrases rather than derived.
vicino keeps its a: vicino a casa, vicino a Roma. English "near the house" has no "to" in it at all, so the missing a is the commonest slip in this module.
Ask where with dove — and in front of è it loses its own vowel and joins on: dov'è. The apostrophe is written every time, and dov'è is one word on the page.

sentences.cue: The book is on the table

words.note: su + il, fused into one word — and the fusion is compulsory: there is no su il. The feminine partner is sulla (su + la), and the same law gives al, nel, alla and nella.
Masculine: il tavolo (one) · i tavoli (more than one).

sentences.trap: English writes "on the" as two words and Italian writes one. It is not a contraction you may choose to expand — sul is the only spelling there is.
sentences.sound: SOOL, one syllable, and TA-vo-lo stressed on the first of three.

mistake.display: Il libro è su il tavolo

sentences.usage: Saying where a thing is, in the plainest sentence the language has.
sentences.mnemonic: su + il squeezes down to sul, and it never comes apart again.

words.note: dove is "where", and in front of è it loses its own e and joins on: dov'è, one word with an apostrophe. Both spellings belong here — dove sono i libri? uses the bare one before a consonant.

sentences.trap: Nothing is inverted and nothing is added: the question word goes to the front and è follows it, welded on. English "where is the book" moves the verb; Italian was never going to.
sentences.sound: do-VEH. The apostrophe is where dove's e used to be, and the accent on è survives the fusion.

variations.cue: Where is the station?
variations.changed: swap what you are looking for — dov'è is the frame

variations.cue: Where are the books?
variations.changed: more than one, so sono — and dove keeps its e in front of a consonant

variations.cue: Where is Anna?
variations.changed: a person instead of a thing; nothing else changes

mistake.why: dove and è do not stand apart in front of each other: they elide into dov'è, apostrophe and all.

sentences.mnemonic: The apostrophe is the vowel that dove gave up.

sentences.cue: There is a book on the table

words.note: "There is" — for one thing existing somewhere: c'è un libro. Written as one word with an apostrophe and not built from anything taught separately: learn it whole, beside its plural partner ci sono.

sentences.trap: c'è says something EXISTS; è says where a known thing is. C'è un libro sul tavolo introduces the book; Il libro è sul tavolo tells you where the book you already know about has got to.
sentences.sound: CHEH. The c before an e is the ch of "church", and the apostrophe stands in for a swallowed i.

variations.cue: There is a cat on the table
variations.changed: swap what exists — c'è does not move for it

variations.display: Non c'è un libro sul tavolo
variations.cue: There isn't a book on the table
variations.changed: non in front of the whole thing, apostrophe and all

variations.cue: There is a pizza in the kitchen
variations.changed: a feminine noun and another place — c'è is unaffected by both

mistake.why: The accent and the apostrophe are both part of the word: c'è. Without them it is not a verb at all.

sentences.usage: Pointing out that something is there — the first half of every set of directions.
sentences.mnemonic: c'è has an apostrophe in front and an accent behind.

sentences.display: Ci sono due libri sul tavolo
sentences.cue: There are two books on the table
sentences.literal: There are two books on-the table

words.note: The plural partner of c'è: more than one thing exists, so the verb goes plural — ci sono due libri. English does the same with "there is" and "there are", so the choice is one you already make.
two. Numbers never change shape for gender or number in Italian: due libri, due case, due caffè.

sentences.trap: Some languages leave the existential invariable however many things there are. Italian does not — c'è for one and ci sono for more, exactly as English splits "there is" from "there are".
sentences.sound: chee-SO-no — ci is "chee", the same soft c as in c'è. due is two syllables, DOO-eh, never one.

variations.cue: There is a book on the table
variations.changed: one thing, so the singular comes back

variations.display: Ci sono due gatti in cucina
variations.cue: There are two cats in the kitchen
variations.changed: swap what exists and where — ci sono holds

variations.display: Non ci sono libri sul tavolo
variations.cue: There aren't any books on the table
variations.changed: non in front, and no article once the count is dropped

mistake.why: Two things exist, so the verb is plural: Ci sono due libri sul tavolo.

sentences.usage: Counting what is in a room.
sentences.mnemonic: One thing, c'è; more than one, ci sono — the same choice English makes.

sentences.cue: The pizza is in the kitchen

words.note: in. It fuses with a following definite article — in + il = nel — but a handful of rooms and places take no article at all after it: in cucina, in bagno, in centro. Those are learned whole.
Feminine: la cucina (one) · le cucine (more than one). It is also the verb "she cooks", and the sentence around it is what tells you which.

sentences.trap: English needs "the kitchen" and Italian does without: in cucina. It is not a rule about rooms in general — in salotto and nel salotto both occur — but a small set of phrases learned as they come.
sentences.sound: ku-CHEE-na. The first c is hard because u follows it; the second is soft because i does. Same letter, two sounds, decided by the vowel behind it.

variations.cue: The cat is in the kitchen
variations.changed: swap what is there — the place phrase is fixed

variations.display: La pizza non è in cucina
variations.cue: The pizza isn't in the kitchen
variations.changed: non in front of è, and nothing else moves

variations.cue: Where is the pizza?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

mistake.display: La pizza è in la cucina
mistake.why: Two things at once: in and la would fuse into nella, and this particular phrase takes no article at all — in cucina.

sentences.usage: Answering "where is it?" about a room in a house.
sentences.mnemonic: in cucina is one phrase, learned whole.

sentences.cue: The bread is on the plate

words.note: in + il, fused. Its feminine partner is nella (in + la), and the same law that gives sul and al gives these.
Masculine: il piatto (one) · i piatti (more than one). Italian puts food IN a plate rather than on it — nel piatto — and the same word means a dish on a menu.

sentences.trap: English puts food ON a plate; Italian puts it IN one. The preposition follows the language's picture of the thing, not a rule you can derive from English.
sentences.sound: NEL, one syllable, and PYAT-to with the double t held — a single t would be a different word.

variations.cue: The pizza is on the plate
variations.changed: swap what is there — nel is untouched

variations.cue: The bread is in the kitchen
variations.changed: a feminine noun WITH its article, so the fusion is nella

variations.display: Il pane non è nel piatto
variations.cue: The bread isn't on the plate
variations.changed: non in front of è

mistake.display: Il pane è in il piatto
mistake.why: in and il fuse: nel. There is no spelling that keeps them apart.

sentences.usage: At a table, looking for something.
sentences.mnemonic: in + il = nel, su + il = sul, a + il = al — one pattern, three prepositions.

words.note: a + il, fused — the third of the same family as sul and nel, and its feminine partner is alla. It is the same a that marks a destination in vado a Roma, meeting an article on the way.
An Italian bar is where you get a coffee in the morning and a pastry with it. It is not a pub, and it is open all day. The word takes no plural ending: un bar, due bar.

sentences.trap: The word is the same and the place is not. Walking into an Italian bar at eight in the morning is what the word is FOR.
sentences.sound: AL, one syllable. BAR has a single tapped r and a short open a — nothing like the long English "bahr".

variations.display: Anna è al bar con Rohan
variations.cue: Anna is at the bar with Rohan
variations.changed: con brings someone else in, behind the place

variations.cue: Anna isn't at the bar
variations.changed: non in front of è; the place phrase holds

variations.cue: Where is the bar?
variations.changed: the question, with the article back to its bare il

mistake.why: a and il fuse: al. Anna è al bar.

sentences.usage: Saying where someone is, in the place Italians most often are.
sentences.mnemonic: a + il = al: the a swallows the i.

sentences.display: Il bar è vicino a casa
sentences.literal: The bar is near to home

words.note: "Near", and the a is part of it: vicino a casa. English "near" carries no preposition, so the a is often dropped. When an article follows, the a fuses with it — vicino al bar, alla stazione.

sentences.trap: English "near the house" has no "to" in it, so nothing in the learner's ear asks for the a. Italian will not do without it.
sentences.sound: vi-CHEE-no — the c before i is soft, the same one as in cucina's second syllable and in c'è.

variations.cue: The station is near home
variations.changed: swap what is near — the phrase is the frame

variations.display: Il bar è vicino a Roma

variations.changed: a city instead of a place, and still no article

variations.display: Il bar non è vicino a casa
variations.cue: The bar isn't near home

mistake.why: vicino keeps its a: Il bar è vicino a casa.

sentences.usage: Directions, and the first thing anyone asks about a flat.

sentences.display: Il gatto è sotto il tavolo
sentences.cue: The cat is under the table

words.note: under, and unlike vicino it needs no a: sotto il tavolo. It does not fuse with the article either — the two words stay apart.
Masculine: il gatto (one) · i gatti (more than one), with gatta for a female cat when it matters.

sentences.trap: Two prepositions in this module, two different habits: vicino needs an a and sotto does not. There is no rule that predicts which; they are learned with the word.
sentences.sound: SOT-to and GAT-to, both with a doubled consonant that is genuinely held longer. The g before a is hard.

variations.display: I gatti sono sotto il tavolo
variations.cue: The cats are under the table

variations.cue: Where is the cat?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

mistake.display: Il gatto è sotto al tavolo
mistake.why: sotto takes the article on its own: sotto il tavolo. It is vicino that needs an a.

sentences.mnemonic: vicino a, but sotto il — each preposition keeps its own habit.

words.note: Feminine: la stazione (one) · le stazioni (more than one). Nearly every Italian noun ending in -zione is feminine, and nearly every one of them has an English twin ending in -tion.
here. Its partner is lì, "there" — which carries an accent, because a bare li would be a different word altogether.

sentences.trap: qui and lì do the pointing in this course. There is another word for "there", là, and it is one accent away from la, the article — which is why this module leaves it alone.
sentences.sound: sta-TSYO-ne — the zi is a "ts" with a glide, and the final -e is pronounced. qui is KWEE: qu is always "kw".

mistake.why: "There" is lì, with its accent. A bare li is a different word, and the accent is what keeps them apart.

sentences.mnemonic: qui is near, lì is far — and lì wears an accent.
